title: Galentines Day

jokes.text: The only thing I am crazy about is a magnificent, pregnant manta ray named Ann Perkins.
jokes.setup: Ben tells Leslie she's gone crazy over obsessing about her friend.
jokes.punchline: Leslie doubles down with an over-the-top, poetic declaration about Ann — calling her a 'magnificent, pregnant manta ray.'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly encapsulates Leslie's hyperbolic adoration of Ann. 'Manta ray' is a specific, weird, vivid choice that lands because of how sincere Leslie sounds. Strong character integration — only Leslie would say this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're crazy.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Am I? Or am I a pregnant manta ray gliding through the ocean of truth, my unborn calf nestled safely in my womb of wisdom?

jokes.text: I am ranking topics of conversation for our next phone call. What do you think should be higher priority? Infinity scarves or whether or not it's worth it for me to get Showtime?
jokes.setup: Leslie is preparing for a phone call with Ann with military-level organization.
jokes.punchline: The 'high priority' topics are trivially mundane — infinity scarves vs. Showtime.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Leslie's obsessive organizational energy applied to friendship minutiae. The comedy is in the gap between her serious tone and the trivial content. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm a great sounding board for female friendship issues. I can talk about anything — whether it's a disagreement over a borrowed sweater, or if one of you saw the other one's ex at the Sweetgreen and didn't tell her.

jokes.text: Plus, every time I start talking to you, five seconds later, I want to jump your bones. — Oh, let's do that instead. — See, that's what I'm talking about.
jokes.setup: Leslie explains why Ben can't replace Ann as a sounding board — she gets distracted.
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately proves her point by suggesting they do that instead, validating her complaint in real time.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured micro-callback within the same scene. Ben self-sabotages Leslie's argument by immediately proving it true, which is efficient and charming. The structure is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I could help with girl talk.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, you'd embarrass yourself. You'd probably overshare about your sex life with Ann.

jokes.text: I always knew there would be a day when I would get through to you and you would love government work. Today is that historic day. — Yes. That is what has happened.
jokes.setup: Ron volunteers to do outdoor surveying, and Leslie interprets this as a breakthrough in his anti-government philosophy.
jokes.punchline: Ron's utterly flat, minimal confirmation is the joke — he's clearly just doing it to be alone outside, and his deadpan 'Yes. That is what has happened.' is perfectly withholding.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Ron Swanson moment. The contrast between Leslie's earnest exuberance and Ron's terse, robotic agreement is beautifully constructed. 'Yes. That is what has happened.' is an extraordinarily economical line — five words that convey absolute deadpan while hiding Ron's actual motive. High character integration: only Ron delivers this this way. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing exactly what Ron is really thinking.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I have to say, I'm really impressed by your enthusiasm for this park survey work.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not doing it for enthusiasm. I'm doing it because the survey has a section where I can write 'None of your business' for every answer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, I know. You're trying to hide it, but I can see it in your eyes. You're falling in love with government.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I am not falling in love with government.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's okay, Ron. This is a safe space. A lot of people come around eventually. You're going to love it here.

jokes.text: I love being a father, but there are a few things I miss. Silence, the absence of noise, one single moment undisturbed by the sounds of a children's TV program called Doc McStuffins. There is no quiet anymore. There is only Doc McStuffins.
jokes.setup: Ron's talking-head explains why he wants to be outside alone.
jokes.punchline: The escalating specificity — not just noise, but specifically Doc McStuffins — and the apocalyptic final line 'There is only Doc McStuffins' deliver the payoff.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'silence' to 'absence of noise' to the singular specific torment of Doc McStuffins is excellently structured. 'There is no quiet anymore. There is only Doc McStuffins.' is genuinely quotable — it has the rhythm of epic tragedy applied to toddler television. Ron Swanson experiencing fatherhood is rich comedic territory, and this is one of the better executions of that theme.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I know you care about this town just as much as I do. You're committed to public service, to making Pawnee better for everyone!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes. That is exactly why I do what I do.

jokes.text: Shotgun! I call shotgun. Where are we going? Doesn't matter. Shotgun. Shotgun on all rides for the rest of the day. For the rest of my life. In any car! Ha ha! I just faced you suckers!
jokes.setup: Andy is assigned to go with Ron on a work errand.
jokes.punchline: Andy's child-like escalation of calling shotgun — from 'this car' to 'rest of my life' to 'any car' — is funny for its runaway enthusiasm and complete disconnection from the stakes.
jokes.explanation: Solid Andy Dwyer character comedy. The joke rides purely on his man-child energy and the escalation structure. Not subtle, but the 'rest of my life / any car' extension earns the laugh. Character integration is high — this is quintessential Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I love government work. It's the solitude, the autonomy, and the endless time to think about nothing.

jokes.text: Is the tent guy left-handed or right-handed? I just need to know which way to part my hair to get us a better price. It's a business theory I'm working on.
jokes.setup: Ben and Tom are heading to negotiate a tent deal.
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'business theory' about hair parting direction and negotiation pricing is completely made-up pseudo-science delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom Haverford hustle-bro pseudoscience. The specificity of hair parting direction as a negotiation tool is delightfully absurd. 'It's a business theory I'm working on' seals it — the confidence is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have two children. If I had known what that entailed, I would have used more protection. Not condoms. A lot more protection. Like a full suit of armor. And I'm not talking about their mother. I'm talking about Daniel Tiger's Neighborhood. That show is on all the time. All the time. I wake up, Daniel Tiger's there. I go to work, Daniel Tiger's there. I come home, Daniel Tiger's there. I go to sleep, I dream about Daniel Tiger. I'm starting to think Daniel Tiger might actually be my son.

jokes.text: A straightforward deal? Why didn't you tell me? I don't have my straightforward deal fedora on me. We gotta stop by my storage unit on the way up.
jokes.setup: Ben says the tent deal should be straightforward.
jokes.punchline: Tom has a dedicated fedora for straightforward deals — kept in a storage unit — implying an entire wardrobe of situational hats.
jokes.explanation: Tightly constructed Tom joke. The specificity ('straightforward deal fedora') and the implication of a whole taxonomy of situational hats in a storage unit is very funny. The rewatch bonus is because viewers can imagine the storage unit full of situational fedoras.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Doc McStuffins has consumed my entire reality. I can no longer distinguish between what is real and what is a children's cartoon about a girl who fixes stuffed animals in her backyard playhouse.

jokes.text: No. Why'd you invite Larry? — He's been doing all the paperwork for this deal. He deserves to come. — Remember you said that when Larry's farting up the car.
jokes.setup: Ben defends inviting Larry on the trip.
jokes.punchline: Tom's prediction — 'when Larry's farting up the car' — is specific, unglamorous, and delivered as near-prophecy.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for a callback payoff later (Larry does fart in the car). The joke here is mild but the rewatch value increases once the prophecy is fulfilled. Somewhat lazy as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Shotgun!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I call shotgun forever. Faced you suckers!

jokes.text: Larry isn't that bad. He's nice. And frankly, I don't care who knows that I said that, as long as no one knows that I said that.
jokes.setup: Ben defends Larry while also being conditioned by office culture to not openly like Larry.
jokes.punchline: The self-contradiction — 'I don't care who knows... as long as no one knows' — is delivered earnestly, revealing Ben's social anxiety about liking the office punching bag.
jokes.explanation: This is a gem of a line. The self-negating logic — 'I don't care who knows... as long as no one knows' — is perfectly economical and deeply character-specific. It captures Ben's fundamentally decent but socially calibrated personality. Highly quotable and it foreshadows his big speech at the end of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so here's what I'm thinking. Right-handed people part their hair on the left side of their head. Left-handed people part their hair on the right side. It's just basic science.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The dominant hand controls the dominant side of the head. It's like a natural flow.

jokes.text: I made a backup plan for the vendor chart in case, you know, yours isn't good.
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Donna and April she'll be busy with her Ann call.
jokes.punchline: She casually mentions she made a backup plan for their work in case it's bad — delivered as an aside, completely unselfconscious.
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient Leslie character joke — her controlling competence expressed as casually offensive confidence. Works well because she doesn't even realize it's rude.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have specific fedoras for different types of business deals. This is my hostile takeover fedora. This is my friendly acquisition fedora. And this... this is my 'I'm about to close a deal that will make me rich beyond my wildest dreams' fedora.

jokes.text: That's exactly what they'd make you say. — Also, no one's making me say this. I am a free woman, untaken, simply going about my business.
jokes.setup: Leslie is leaving a voicemail for Ann insisting she hasn't been kidnapped.
jokes.punchline: She anticipates and preemptively addresses Ann's skepticism ('that's what they'd make you say'), then doubles down with the absurdist 'untaken, simply going about my business.'
jokes.explanation: The self-refuting escalation ('that's exactly what they'd make you say') is clever and the continuation 'untaken, simply going about my business' is a funny phrase. The bit demonstrates that Leslie and Ann have an established shared language of absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, but here's the thing about Larry being nice: if he's nice to me, he's gonna want to hang out with me. And if he hangs out with me, he's gonna eventually do something weird like fall asleep at my dinner table or pee on my couch.

jokes.text: I'm listening to Jaleel Or No Deal. It's a podcast where the kid who played Urkel reviews old Deal Or No Deal episodes. It's pointless, and I love it.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to chat with Donna at work.
jokes.punchline: The podcast name is a perfect portmanteau ('Jaleel Or No Deal') and the meta-description — 'it's pointless, and I love it' — is an honest, funny self-assessment.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best one-liners. 'Jaleel Or No Deal' is a genuinely clever pun, and the description is so perfectly crafted — the specificity (Urkel/Steve Urkel actor reviewing Deal or No Deal) combined with Donna's self-aware 'it's pointless, and I love it' makes this a minor masterpiece of character economy. Highly quotable. This is close to the 8.0 anchor level.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Larry is a genuinely nice guy. I don't care what anyone says.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? Larry's the worst.

jokes.text: Ew, my husband, weirdo. Can I get back to work now? Thanks. Bye.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks April who she's crushing on in an attempt to bond.
jokes.punchline: April's complete deflation of the question ('ew, my husband') plus her rapid-fire dismissal ('Thanks. Bye.') is perfectly April.
jokes.explanation: Economy here is extraordinary — 'ew, my husband, weirdo' is five words that say everything about April's character. The speed of the dismissal ('Can I get back to work now? Thanks. Bye.') is the perfect April cadence. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have a backup plan for Ann. Actually, I have seventeen backup plans for Ann. I've laminated them. There's one where I convince her that her apartment building is being demolished, so she has to move in with me. Another one where I anonymously tell her that her job is being outsourced to India, so she'll need a new best friend to help her through the transition. I've also—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, no, forget everything I just said.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why would you say that out loud?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, this is your fault for being here and listening to me.

jokes.text: Work? You can work whenever. Except for now, because now is lady time.
jokes.setup: April asks to get back to work.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's rebuke of 'work' as a priority is funny coming from the most work-obsessed person in Pawnee.
jokes.explanation: Solid joke. The irony of Leslie deprioritizing work is the core gag. 'Lady time' is a funny phrase. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's Ann. I'm fine. I'm not kidnapped. I know that's your first assumption about everything, but I promise you, I'm okay.

jokes.text: You sound like a tampon commercial.
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'now is lady time.'
jokes.punchline: April's flat, perfectly timed comeback.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words, maximum deflation. April's deadpan delivery of exactly the right comeback is great. The visual of Leslie enthusiastically saying 'lady time' does genuinely resemble a tampon commercial. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I haven't been replaced by a clone or an alien or whatever you think.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's exactly what a clone would say.

jokes.text: I need an Ann who lives in Pawnee, and there is no one obvious candidate, so I will test them out on the ultimate battlefield of female friendship — Galentine's day brunch.
jokes.setup: Leslie explains her plan in a talking-head confessional.
jokes.punchline: Calling a brunch 'the ultimate battlefield of female friendship' is Leslie's characteristic hyperbole. The hunt for an Ann replacement is also inherently funny.
jokes.explanation: The premise of the B-plot is itself the joke here. 'Ultimate battlefield' applied to brunch is good Leslie hyperbole. Sets up the episode's comedy engine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Donna, hey! So I was thinking we could hang out sometime. You know, do some cool stuff. Maybe go to... Club Rad? Or Flavor Town? I just made those up, but they sound fun, right?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Leslie, no.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What about Punchline Palace? That's where all the hip people go. We could be hip together!

jokes.text: It will be a women's-only marathon bonding session with tons of whipped cream. Side note, do not Google that phrase.
jokes.setup: Leslie describes Galentine's Day in glowing terms, ending with 'tons of whipped cream.'
jokes.punchline: She then immediately acknowledges the double entendre by warning them not to Google it — a rare moment of Leslie self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: The 'do not Google that phrase' tag is well-timed and self-aware. It works because it's a rare moment of Leslie clocking her own unintentional double entendre. Good structure: setup, accidental innuendo, acknowledgment.

jokes.text: Can you rub any kind of mud on yourself to prevent predator from seeing you with his thermal heat signature sight, or is it more-- Ow! That sucks.
jokes.setup: Andy asks Ron a serious-sounding question about the movie Predator mid-survey.
jokes.punchline: The philosophical inquiry into Predator thermal vision is interrupted by Andy apparently hurting himself — the serious question collapses into physical comedy.
jokes.explanation: The bit works on multiple levels — Andy's genuine intellectual curiosity about Predator is funny on its own, and its sudden interruption by physical injury is perfectly Andy. The injury becomes a plot point (tooth), making this efficient setup.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hey little mama, you want to hear some hot goss about the parks department?

jokes.text: Oh, whoa. Five-second rule. No, ahh.
jokes.setup: Andy has apparently knocked out or damaged a tooth.
jokes.punchline: Andy's instinct is to invoke the five-second rule about his tooth — treating it like dropped food — before someone stops him.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character-specific joke. Andy applying the five-second rule to his own tooth is so perfectly him — childlike, gross, immediate — that it earns a big laugh. The quick denial ('No, ahh') from Ron or the situation makes it land even better. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So who are you crushing on?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ugh, gross. Ben.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, Larry. Your tuna fish sandwich stunk up my suit. — Gayle made it for me. — Irrelevant.
jokes.setup: Tom is upset about the smell of Larry's sandwich.
jokes.punchline: Larry's defense — 'Gayle made it for me' — is sweet and irrelevant; Tom's one-word dismissal 'Irrelevant' is perfectly clipped.
jokes.explanation: Efficient little joke. Larry's pathetic defense referencing Gayle (his inexplicably beautiful wife, referenced later) and Tom's rapid-fire dismissal work well. 'Irrelevant' as a one-word punchline is snappy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Now is lady time.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You mean like a feminine hygiene product commercial?

jokes.text: I take tents pretty seriously, Ben, I'm a tent guy. I got over 1,300 tents in this warehouse alone. 900 of those are over 2,000 square feet, 80 of 'em are striped, and exactly 4 of 'em were once rented by Miss Rene Russo.
jokes.setup: Harvey is establishing his tent credentials.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from impressive statistics to the weirdly specific Rene Russo rental factoid is the joke — the serious tone applied to tent renting is also inherently funny.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed escalation. Harvey's serious recitation of tent statistics is funny on its own, but the pivot to 'exactly 4 of them were once rented by Miss Rene Russo' is perfect — specific, celebrity, oddly formal ('Miss'). The 'No doy' follow-up is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ann is the worst. She's a human snake. She has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. Every word that comes out of her mouth is a lie and an attack on everyone around her.

jokes.text: Oh, thanks. I just got back from a solo trip to Rome. I was gonna go with my boyfriend, but he couldn't come because he decided to stay with his wife.
jokes.setup: Leslie compliments Shauna's tan at the Galentine's Day brunch.
jokes.punchline: Shauna casually reveals she was dating a married man, delivered completely without self-awareness as if it's unremarkable.
jokes.explanation: The structure is tight: cheerful setup ('I just got back from Rome') into a quietly devastating reveal ('he decided to stay with his wife'). Shauna's complete lack of self-awareness is the joke, and the economy is excellent. Leslie's 'Oof' reaction seals it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're having a women's-only marathon bonding session with tons of whipped cream.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I just realized how that sounds when you google it.

jokes.text: Rome's played out. Have y'all been to Kuala Lumpur? — When did you go to Asia? — I go all the time. Where do you think I got that crystal Buddha head above my jacuzzi?
jokes.setup: Shauna mentions Rome was great.
jokes.punchline: Donna casually one-ups her with Kuala Lumpur and a jacuzzi with a crystal Buddha head, delivered as completely unremarkable.
jokes.explanation: Great Donna moment — her casual worldliness and prosperity is a running character trait, and 'crystal Buddha head above my jacuzzi' is a perfectly Donna detail. The one-upping of Rome with Kuala Lumpur is also characteristic.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So wait, if I put my card in the ATM and I ask for $200, where does the money come from?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Does the ATM just... have $200 sitting in there? And what happens when it runs out? Does someone come refill it?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Or is there like, a giant ATM somewhere that all the other ATMs get money from? Like an ATM mother ship?

jokes.text: Prospects for new Pawnee best friend. Donna Meagle: confident, worldly, we go way back. April Ludgate: vivid imagination, young, and vibrant. Shauna Malwae-Tweep: pretty, fragile, makes terrible life decisions. A real fixer-upper, but look, it's not like Ann was doing so hot when I met her.
jokes.setup: Leslie's talking-head confessional evaluating the Galentine's Day attendees as Ann replacement candidates.
jokes.punchline: Shauna being described as 'pretty, fragile, makes terrible life decisions — a real fixer-upper' plus Leslie's self-aware admission that Ann wasn't great either is the payoff.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured talking-head. The escalation from positive descriptors to 'makes terrible life decisions' for Shauna, followed by the undercut 'it's not like Ann was doing so hot when I met her' is smart writing. The rankings frame is both funny and revealing of Leslie's character.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What if he's not an ATM guy? What if he's a guy who stands in front of ATMs and tells you that you're making a mistake?

jokes.text: Ethel Beavers. Bit of a dark horse. Crotchety, but probably wise. And then we got Evelyn, aka fake Ann. I don't know her last name. Honestly, we just needed bodies.
jokes.setup: Continuation of Leslie's friend-candidate confessional.
jokes.punchline: 'Fake Ann' and 'we just needed bodies' is brutally honest — the contrast between the warmth of Galentine's Day and Leslie's clinical assessment is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Fake Ann' and 'we just needed bodies' are dark and funny, especially given the warm framing of Galentine's Day. The 'I don't know her last name' detail is a nice additional beat of Leslie's obliviousness to her own behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so in Predator, the Predator comes to Earth to hunt humans for sport, right? But like, how does he even know where to go? Does he have a GPS? And when he's hunting, does he follow the Geneva Convention? Because I feel like there's gotta be some intergalactic hunting laws, you know? Also, why doesn't he just use a gun like a normal person? Why's he gotta be all fancy with the wrist blades and the cloaking technology? That seems like overkill. And another thing—

jokes.text: Well, for live tweeting, it's Scandal. For binge watching, it's Scandal. But for fashion, it's actually Scandal. My answer is Scandal.
jokes.setup: The Galentine's Day Q&A asks for favorite TV show.
jokes.punchline: Donna's answer builds in apparent variety (three different categories) only to land on the same answer three times, capped with a deadpan summary.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect structure. The fake-out of three different criteria all resolving to 'Scandal' is a classic rule-of-three subversion where the third element isn't the surprise — the callback to the first answer IS the joke. 'My answer is Scandal' as the unnecessary summation is a brilliant button. Highly quotable and one of the episode's best jokes. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh no, I broke my tooth! Five second rule!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not how the five second rule works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's my mouth, April. My rules.

jokes.text: Ooh, I love watching Russian traffic accidents on YouTube while I play children's music at the wrong RPM.
jokes.setup: April answers the 'favorite TV show' question.
jokes.punchline: The specific combination — Russian dashcam crashes + children's music at wrong speed — is perfectly April: morbid, strange, weirdly specific.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. The visual of April watching Russian traffic accidents while playing distorted children's music is so specific and so perfectly April Ludgate that it transcends the question it's answering. The 'wrong RPM' detail is brilliant — it's not that she plays disturbing music, she plays innocent children's music wrongly, making it disturbing. High originality and character integration. One of the episode's standout jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. What is that smell? Did you bring fish? You brought fish to the office? Larry, that is a violation of the Geneva Convention.

jokes.text: I like beauty pageants. Everyone is so happy and perfect.
jokes.setup: Ethel the elderly clerk answers the TV show question.
jokes.punchline: The sweet, simple, slightly sad sincerity of her love of beauty pageants because 'everyone is so happy and perfect' is unexpectedly touching and funny.
jokes.explanation: Mild joke, works mainly by contrast with the other answers. The sweet obliviousness of the response is gently funny but doesn't have great structure or originality.

jokes.text: I like Diagnosis Murder. And skin flicks.
jokes.setup: Evelyn (fake Ann) answers the TV show question.
jokes.punchline: The pivot from wholesome 'Diagnosis Murder' to 'skin flicks' is sudden and funny, especially from a character we know nothing about.
jokes.explanation: Effective misdirection — 'Diagnosis Murder' sets up a wholesome older-person answer, and 'skin flicks' lands as a shock. The economy is excellent. Limited character integration since Evelyn is a one-scene placeholder, but the structure works.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: I just got back from Rome. It was amazing. I spent two weeks there just exploring, eating pasta, living my best life.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: And I met this really great guy. We've been dating for a few months now. He's so romantic, always taking me to these beautiful places.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: The only thing is... he's married. But it's fine, because his wife doesn't understand him.

jokes.text: The correct answer for favorite TV show is Friday Night Lights. — The correct answer?
jokes.setup: After everyone gives their TV answers, Leslie announces the 'correct' answer.
jokes.punchline: Leslie declaring an objective correct answer to a subjective preference question reveals her controlling nature — and everyone's baffled reaction validates the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Good character joke. Leslie's certainty that there's a 'correct' answer to a subjective question is a great expression of her personality, and Friday Night Lights as the specific answer (which pays off later in the Ann conversation) is smart writing.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I don't need to travel to Asia. I have everything I need at home. I got a sauna, a steam room, a hot tub, and a rainfall shower that cost more than your car.

jokes.text: A tent without flaps is basically a parachute. — An unfolding charge? A noise damage waiver? How can noise damage tents? — Shh. Keep your voice down, please, there's tents here.
jokes.setup: Ben and Tom are disputing bogus contract line items.
jokes.punchline: Harvey's defense of tents being sensitive to noise ('keep your voice down, please, there's tents here') is a perfect absurdist escalation — treating the tents as if they're sleeping patients.
jokes.explanation: 'Keep your voice down, please, there's tents here' is a genuinely inspired absurdist line. Harvey is treating the tents like hospital patients or sleeping children — the anthropomorphization is sudden and committed. High originality. The setup of bogus charges makes it earned. One of the episode's standout lines.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you are such a good friend, but you are my only friend. And I don't think I can afford to be that picky.

jokes.text: For every line item that you two idiots disagree with, there's gonna be a $50 discussion surcharge. — $400. — A discussion surcharge? That's nuts. — $450.
jokes.setup: Harvey introduces a surcharge for every objection raised.
jokes.punchline: The counter ticking up in real time as they react to the surcharge (thus incurring more surcharges) is a perfectly constructed trap.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural comedy. The joke is a logic trap: objecting to the surcharge triggers the surcharge. 'A discussion surcharge? That's nuts.' → '$450' is perfectly timed. The self-defeating spiral is elegant and reminiscent of the best sitcom negotiation comedy. Strong structure score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is Evelyn. She's here to make the rest of us look good.

jokes.text: Wait, wait. Let me try one more thing. [Tom parts hair to other side] — What's the price now? — $80 more. I liked it better the other way.
jokes.setup: Tom established his hair-parting business theory earlier.
jokes.punchline: Tom actually tries the theory and it makes things worse — Harvey even notices and has a preference.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback execution. The callback to the hair-parting theory is both a payoff and a subversion — it doesn't work, but Harvey's admission that 'I liked it better the other way' suggests it had SOME effect, just not the right one. 'Does have an effect, though' from Ben is a nice understated button. Well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have some friendship questions for you. They're just for fun, totally casual.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But I should warn you, if you answer wrong, I will be very upset and reconsider our entire friendship.

jokes.text: All I wanted was two hours where I got to forget that I was a parent.
jokes.setup: Ron is in a dentist's waiting room with Andy, presumably filling out forms for him.
jokes.punchline: Ron's weary admission that he just wanted two hours of peace, now spent essentially parenting a grown man, is the quiet culmination of the Doc McStuffins setup.
jokes.explanation: Strong callback payoff. Ron escaped to the wilderness to avoid parenting and ended up parenthesized Andy in a waiting room. The economy of 'I got to forget I was a parent' — without saying Andy is acting like a child — is excellent. Very Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Scandal. It's my favorite show. It's my favorite book. It's my favorite movie. It's my favorite food. It's my favorite time of day.

jokes.text: Ron, look. I found all three differences. — Those are two completely different pictures.
jokes.setup: Andy is doing a 'spot the difference' puzzle in a waiting room magazine.
jokes.punchline: Andy is proud of completing the puzzle — but the pictures are completely different images, not a spot-the-difference pair.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical Andy joke. The image is vivid even without seeing it — Andy earnestly completing what he thinks is a puzzle, only for Ron to flatly note they're completely different pictures. High character integration (only Andy does this) and strong structure. Gets better when Andy's magazine cheating is confessed to at the end of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I like to watch depressing foreign films while eating cubed cheese and drinking boxed wine. It's called 'having culture.'

jokes.text: I've gotten two annulments. One for pleasure, and one to cap off a long con I was running against Keith Sweat.
jokes.setup: Wild card option at Galentine's Day — anyone reveals anything about their life.
jokes.punchline: Donna has two annulments — one for pleasure, one as a Keith Sweat long con. The specificity of 'Keith Sweat' and the concept of an annulment for 'pleasure' are both individually funny.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. 'One for pleasure, and one to cap off a long con I was running against Keith Sweat' is exceptional on every level. The parallelism of the two reasons is perfectly structured, the specificity of Keith Sweat (a real 90s R&B singer) is inspired, and 'long con' applied to an annulment is delightfully dark and absurd. The entire Donna mythology is enriched. This rivals the 8.0 anchor — in fact, it surpasses it in originality. The 'one for pleasure' framing is genuinely shocking. Highly quotable, essentially a perfect joke.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: I need to watch something that makes me feel happy. My life is a mess. I've made terrible choices. I'm aging. Nothing good is happening to me. So I need TV to give me that artificial happiness that I'm not getting in real life.

jokes.text: Wow. Ethel, have you-- Okay, Ethel's asleep.
jokes.setup: After Donna's dramatic revelation, Leslie turns to Ethel for hers.
jokes.punchline: Ethel has fallen asleep — the visual beats the dialogue.
jokes.explanation: Classic old-person-falls-asleep gag. Not original or sophisticated, but it's efficiently deployed and comes right after Donna's big joke so it doesn't overstay its welcome. Functions as a transition beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ethel
dialogue.line: Oh, I watch all sorts of things. Game shows, the news, sometimes a little pornography before bed. It helps me sleep.

jokes.text: I'm writing a memoir based on my blog. It's called Tweeping Up Appearances, and it's about my journey to find happiness by smiling through the pain.
jokes.setup: Shauna takes her turn at the wild card reveal.
jokes.punchline: 'Tweeping Up Appearances' is a groan-worthy but committed pun (tweeting + keeping up appearances), and the memoir's theme is the perfect encapsulation of Shauna's sad-optimism character.
jokes.explanation: The pun is clever (tweep = Twitter user + keeping up appearances) and the subtitle 'smiling through the pain' is a funny summary of Shauna's entire existence. Good character joke that deepens her in one line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone just said their favorite TV shows, and I want you to know that this was actually a test.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And there was a right answer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was Parks and Recreation.

jokes.text: 'Friendship rankings.' What's that? — It's not what it sounds like. — It's simply a way for me to figure out which one of you is the best.
jokes.setup: Donna spots Leslie's notebook with 'Friendship Rankings' written on it.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's instant capitulation — 'it's not what it sounds like... it's simply a way to figure out which one of you is the best' — perfectly confirms the obvious, compounding the offense.
jokes.explanation: The immediate walk-back that confirms the accusation is a great structural choice. 'It's not what it sounds like' followed by an exact description of what it sounds like is a classic but well-executed bit. Strong character integration — Leslie's obliviousness to her own rudeness is authentic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What is a 'flap tax'?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know, but apparently Harvey charges it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This contract is insane. Who charges a flap tax?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A very creative accountant.

jokes.text: That's messed up. — Yeah, that is really lame, and I'm leaving. — You're better than that, Knope. — Donna, why are you angry? You were in first place.
jokes.setup: The Galentine's Day guests react to discovering Leslie has been ranking them.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's attempted pacification of Donna — 'you were in first place' — completely misses the point and makes everything worse.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's 'you were in first place' as damage control is wonderfully oblivious — she genuinely doesn't understand why the rankings are offensive, and thinks informing Donna of her standing will help. Very strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Harvey
dialogue.line: A flap tax? That's when you tax the flaps on envelopes. It's a new revenue stream for the city. Look, it's simple economics - every time someone licks an envelope, that's a taxable event. We could raise thousands of dollars a year. Thousands!

jokes.text: ...brunch. / Leave the bag.
jokes.setup: Guests are leaving after the friendship rankings reveal
jokes.punchline: 'Leave the bag' — Leslie telling Evelyn to leave behind whatever she brought reveals the purely transactional nature of 'fake Ann's' inclusion
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum character revelation. 'Leave the bag' tells you everything about Leslie's relationship with Evelyn — she was there for the food/supplies, not the person.

jokes.text: Gayle always has me do the windshield. She likes to stand behind me and watch. According to her, it's the best view.
jokes.setup: Larry is wiping down the car windshield at a gas station.
jokes.punchline: Larry shares that his beautiful wife enjoys watching him do this because 'it's the best view' — an unexpected affirmation that underscores the running joke of Gayle's inexplicable devotion.
jokes.explanation: The joke deepens the Gayle/Larry dynamic — she loves watching Larry do something as mundane as wipe a windshield because she finds him attractive. Given Larry's status as the office punching bag, this is both sweet and funny. Sets up the later joke about Gayle's inexplicable gorgeousness.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, you're charging us for this?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, what is this fee for?

dialogue.speaker: Harvey
dialogue.line: That's my disagreement fee. You disagreed with me, so that'll be $50.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Harvey
dialogue.line: Oh, now you're disagreeing with me about the disagreement fee? That's another $50.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. I'm just not used to people from the office asking me things. It's kind of scary. But in a good way, though.
jokes.setup: Ben asks genuinely how Larry's family is doing.
jokes.punchline: Larry's admission that he's scared by human interest from coworkers — 'in a good way' — is both funny and quietly devastating.
jokes.explanation: This lands as both a laugh and a small gut-punch. Larry's conditioning — surprise at basic human decency — tells us everything about his office life. 'In a good way, though' is the perfect tag: he's trying to be positive about something that should be normal. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so I'm telling you, the hair part is crucial. You part your hair the right way, you part your life the right way.

dialogue.speaker: Harvey
dialogue.line: That doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, no, hear me out. I've been doing a deep side part for three weeks now, and my business ventures have been down 40%.

dialogue.speaker: Harvey
dialogue.line: So it's not working.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Not yet. I just need to find the perfect part. The part is out there, and when I find it, everything's gonna click.

jokes.text: Aw, man, did I miss a Larry fart? — Oh, no, uh, we were just-- Yeah, Tom. Yeah, I-I really ripped one. Didn't I, Ben? — Yeah. Yeah, it was loud. Smells like a hippopotamus took a dump on a skunk.
jokes.setup: Tom arrives to find Ben and Larry having a nice moment. Tom immediately assumes it was a fart moment.
jokes.punchline: Larry and Ben cover the genuine moment by conspiring in the fart lie — and Ben's description ('smells like a hippopotamus took a dump on a skunk') is extravagant and specific.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff with a twist — Tom's prophecy is confirmed, but the fart didn't happen; they're covering a genuine bonding moment WITH a fake fart. This adds an emotional layer to the comedy. Ben's simile is a classic of the genre. Rewatch value because you understand the cover-up.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me my teeth are in my mouth? I thought they were stored somewhere else, like a safe deposit box or something.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And flossing is... what, a dance move? No? You do it with string? Why would you put string in your mouth?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Also, I've been using a comb on my teeth this whole time. Is that wrong?

jokes.text: I don't know, I think my tooth looks fine just like this. — Well, my grandmother was missing that tooth, and she was the most beautiful woman on her oil rig.
jokes.setup: Andy doesn't want to go back to the dentist after leaving.
jokes.punchline: Ron's encouragement comes in the form of a grandmother who was beautiful 'on her oil rig' — the specific, unusual setting elevates a straightforward compliment into something strange and Ron-specific.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed Ron joke. He's trying to be encouraging using the only reference points he has — his manly, rugged family. 'The most beautiful woman on her oil rig' implies a specific, physically demanding world that is completely Ron's frame of reference. The comedy is in the qualifier. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I love Andy. But I need a break from him. A parental break.

jokes.text: That's why you know even though you're not my dad, you're like an old brother to me. Like a cool uncle, but old. Like a grandpa. But cool like a son.
jokes.setup: Andy thanks Ron for taking care of him.
jokes.punchline: Andy's attempt to define their relationship devolves into a contradictory word salad — each clarification makes it worse, ending in the nonsensical 'cool like a son.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke. Each attempted clarification creates a new contradiction: 'old brother' → 'cool uncle but old' → 'grandpa' → 'cool like a son.' The final inversion (a son being the comparison for coolness when you're talking to someone older) is absurdly logical in Andy's head. Highly quotable and very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron, I just finished this crossword puzzle!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's a word search.

jokes.text: What, you're charging us for coffee? What kind of a business-- uh-oh.
jokes.setup: Ben and Tom stop at a coffee place after leaving the tent warehouse.
jokes.punchline: Tom begins complaining about being charged for coffee and then recognizes they've walked into another Harvey-owned business.
jokes.explanation: Good structural moment — the running gag of Harvey's business empire extends in a surprising direction. The 'uh-oh' is perfectly timed anticipatory comedy. Sets up the next Harvey confrontation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Donna, I need you to tell me something real. Something true about your life that you've never told anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I was married to Seal for three weeks in the '90s.

jokes.text: That's right, dickweed. You wanna talk deal? Because my prices have gone up ever so slightly since I saw you last.
jokes.setup: Tom and Ben realize Harvey owns the gas station
jokes.punchline: 'Dickweed' as a casual greeting combined with 'ever so slightly' (classic understatement for presumably massive price hikes) continues Harvey's villainous absurdism
jokes.explanation: Harvey remains a consistently funny character. 'Dickweed' is a funny word choice and 'ever so slightly' is a good understatement. Solid villain-comic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: The terrible pun title and depressing subject matter

jokes.text: That's right, dickweed. You wanna talk deal?
jokes.setup: Tom and Ben discover Harvey owns the coffee shop too.
jokes.punchline: Harvey's casual 'dickweed' greeting and immediate pivot to deal talk is a great character beat.
jokes.explanation: Harvey as a villain is elevated by his completely casual use of 'dickweed' — it's not even aggressive, just how he talks. The economy of the line is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so I ranked my friends. Ann is number one because she's my best friend and soulmate. Tom is number two because he's fun and loyal, even if he makes terrible decisions. Ben is number three because he's dependable and attractive. And Jerry... Jerry is number four because he's Jerry.

jokes.text: Yeah, I'm calling Tent Emporium right now. — Tent Emporium. How can I help you, buttface?
jokes.setup: Tom threatens to call a competitor.
jokes.punchline: Harvey answers as Tent Emporium — his own company — and greets Tom with 'buttface.'
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent — Tom's bluff is immediately and perfectly countered. 'Buttface' as the customer greeting is the right amount of absurd. The timing of the phone being answered before Tom finishes dialing (implied) is good visual comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm not mad. I'm just... I thought we were closer than that.

jokes.text: Yes. I own every tent store in Southern Indiana. Tent Town, Rent Ten Tents, the Tent Offensive, and Ace Tentura Tent Detective.
jokes.setup: Tom and Ben try every competitor; Harvey answers as each one.
jokes.punchline: The list of store names escalates beautifully: 'Rent Ten Tents' (tongue-twister), 'the Tent Offensive' (dark historical reference), 'Ace Tentura Tent Detective' (pun on Ace Ventura).
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top two jokes. The list of tent store names is genuinely inspired comedy writing. 'Rent Ten Tents' as a tongue-twister name, 'the Tent Offensive' as a dark WWII pun (Tet Offensive), and 'Ace Tentura Tent Detective' as a multi-layered pun (Ace Ventura + Tenura/tent + Detective) represent three different comedic registers in rapid succession. The escalation in absurdity is perfectly structured, and the commitment to the bit is total. Highly quotable, strong rewatch value. This is a top-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, Gayle really appreciates my physique. She says my love handles are like... well, let's just say she has very specific preferences.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I didn't need to know that.

jokes.text: I also own a Chick-fil-A franchise, but that's not doing so hot right now. Whatever.
jokes.setup: Harvey lists his tent empire.
jokes.punchline: Harvey casually mentions his Chick-fil-A is underperforming — a topical joke referencing the brand's controversies — delivered as complete afterthought.
jokes.explanation: The Chick-fil-A aside is a sharp topical joke — the brand was facing boycotts around 2014 over its charitable contributions controversy. The 'whatever' dismissal is perfect casual deflection. The joke works without knowing the context but lands better with it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So Larry, how was your weekend?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It was... it was good. Why do you ask?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't know, just making conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Nobody ever asks me that.

jokes.text: You've reached the Tentagon. How can I help you, buttface?
jokes.setup: Tom tries yet another tent competitor.
jokes.punchline: 'The Tentagon' (Pentagon) is the final and best name in the list, answered with Harvey's signature 'buttface' greeting.
jokes.explanation: 'The Tentagon' is the perfect topper to the store names list — the Pentagon reference adds a quasi-governmental authority that fits Harvey's dominance of the local tent market. 'Buttface' repeated as the greeting is now a running gag callback. The economy of a single word ('Tentagon') doing so much work is exceptional. One of the episode's best individual lines.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It wasn't Ben, it was me. I farted.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, and it smelled like... old eggs mixed with a tire fire at a fish factory.

jokes.text: Although when I was in college I found out that my dad had a second family. Well, we were the second family, technically.
jokes.setup: Harvey and the team try to find common ground — Harvey reveals he's an only child.
jokes.punchline: Harvey's self-correction — 'we were the second family, technically' — is a dark revelation delivered with total equanimity.
jokes.explanation: The self-correction is the joke — Harvey starts with 'I'm an only child' and immediately undermines it. The casual delivery of a fairly dark family revelation is Harvey's character in miniature. Good economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My grandmother had a broken tooth for like forty years. She just owned it. She'd smile real big at family dinners and everyone would just be like, 'There it is.' It became part of her identity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But then one day she was working on an oil rig in the Gulf of Mexico and a freak accident happened. Tooth went flying right into a pelican's mouth.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We never saw her again. The pelican took her out to sea.

jokes.text: Ann had her baby! Wow, this has been fun. The bill is already paid.
jokes.setup: Harvey and the team are trying to find common ground, discussing college.
jokes.punchline: Ben sees the news about Ann's baby and immediately ends the meeting — the news is so important it instantly vaporizes the negotiation context.
jokes.explanation: Solid reaction beat. Ben's efficient wrap-up ('The bill is already paid') while announcing the baby news is a good character moment that prioritizes the emotional storyline. Functionally funny transition.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron is like... he's like my dad. But if my dad was cool. So he's like my cool dad.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No wait, he's more like my older brother. My cooler older brother who teaches me stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, he's like my uncle. You know, the uncle who shows up to Thanksgiving and everyone's like, 'Oh, Uncle Ron's here!' And then he just sits there not saying anything.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Or... or maybe he's my grandfather? Like, the wise grandfather figure who doesn't really care about anything but somehow you still respect him?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, I got it. He's my wife. Ron is my wife.

jokes.text: May I gently suggest that you check out Chris Traeger's wonderful therapist Dr. Richard Nygard. Although there is a tiny part of me that always thought it was just Chris talking into a mirror.
jokes.setup: Ben is giving Shauna some unsolicited but kind advice before rushing off.
jokes.punchline: The aside — 'I always thought it was just Chris talking into a mirror' — is a perfectly sharp character observation about Chris's extreme narcissism/self-help obsession.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant throwaway line about an absent character. The implication that Chris's therapist might just be Chris talking into a mirror is a perfectly calibrated observation about his character — his relentless positivity and self-focus make this entirely plausible. High originality for a one-liner about a supporting character. Very quotable.

dialogue.line: His immediate hostility and price manipulation

jokes.text: No way. I'm not going back there. I already won all the magazine mazes. — Don't worry. It's gonna be fine. — Fine. Let me just wolf down this peanut brittle real quick. — Why would you do that? — Oh, right. 'Cause calories.
jokes.setup: Andy needs to go back to the dentist for his broken tooth.
jokes.punchline: Andy's non-sequitur reason ('I already won all the magazine mazes') followed immediately by him trying to eat peanut brittle on a broken tooth, with the most Andy possible justification ('cause calories') — is a perfect Andy sequence.
jokes.explanation: The callback to winning the mazes is excellent, and 'cause calories' as the entire justification for eating jaw-destroying candy on a broken tooth is one of the purest Andy Dwyer jokes in the episode. The escalation — refusal → peanut brittle → 'cause calories' — is well-paced. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Harvey
dialogue.line: I own all the tent stores in this city. Started with 'Harvey's Tents,' then 'Tent City Harvey,' then 'Harvey's Tent Emporium,' then 'The Tent Dimension,' then 'Harvey's Tentacle Warehouse'—wait, that's not right. 'Tentacles of Harvey.' No. 'Harvey's House of Tents.' 'Tent Hospital.' 'Tent Intensive Care.' 'Tent Morgue.' I don't actually own any tent stores.

jokes.text: We're dead. The only tent store this guy doesn't own is 300 miles away. — Oh, hang on. Here's a place that might work. It's called Sweaty Roger's Pants Tent. — Oh, no, you can't rent tents there.
jokes.setup: Tom and Ben are desperate, unable to find a tent supplier Harvey doesn't own.
jokes.punchline: Tom finds 'Sweaty Roger's Pants Tent' as a potential option, and Ben immediately shoots it down — both the name and the immediate dismissal are the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Sweaty Roger's Pants Tent' is a funny name on its own, but Ben's immediate 'oh no, you can't rent tents there' raises the question of WHY while closing it down. The joke implies a whole sordid story without explaining it. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm going to open a tent store. This time it'll work.

dialogue.speaker: Harvey
dialogue.line: I already own that one too.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? How?

dialogue.speaker: Harvey
dialogue.line: I bought it. I own all the tent stores in Pawnee. I'm basically a Pentagon.

jokes.text: Whoa! Larry, this is great stuff. Never thought I would say it, but I'm a genius for making you stay outside and do a menial task. — Couldn't agree more. You did it, Tom.
jokes.setup: Larry discovers Harvey's code violations from his 'menial' parking lot task.
jokes.punchline: Tom takes full credit for creating the situation that led to Larry's discovery, and Ben dryly validates him ('You did it, Tom') despite Tom having done nothing.
jokes.explanation: Good Tom character joke — his ability to claim credit for things he didn't do with complete sincerity is a core trait. Ben's deadpan 'You did it, Tom' is the right understated response.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you're an only child too?

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: Yeah, my parents decided one was enough.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Mine too! I always felt like I missed out on sibling bonding.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: I mean, my parents fought constantly, so I mostly just hid in my room and pretended they didn't exist.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh... okay. That's darker than where I was going with this.

jokes.text: Nobody can match your ethnic hybrid energy.
jokes.setup: Leslie is on the phone with Ann, explaining why no one at work can replace her.
jokes.punchline: 'Ethnic hybrid energy' as a compliment is uniquely Leslie — well-meaning but oddly specific in a way that's almost backhanded.
jokes.explanation: Very Leslie — the awkward specificity of 'ethnic hybrid energy' as a compliment lands because it comes from a place of genuine love. The show has always used Leslie's oblivious compliments to Ann as a recurring bit, and this is a solid entry.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You should really see Chris's therapist. She's amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wait, I don't have a therapist.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Friday Night Lights? I am more of a Riggins girl, and you lean Saracen. — Yeah, 'cause Riggins is a criminal. — He took the fall for his brother.
jokes.setup: Ann uses FNL character preferences as a proxy for their different personalities.
jokes.punchline: The FNL debate is treated with the same seriousness as the friendship conversation — Leslie's certainty that Riggins is a criminal is the callback to the 'correct answer' joke.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the FNL 'correct answer' pays off beautifully here — now we see the Riggins/Saracen divide as a real point of contention between Leslie and Ann. The debate itself is funny because it's about fiction, but the emotional stakes are real. 'Riggins is a criminal' vs. 'he took the fall for his brother' is a perfect microcosm of their friendship differences.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: My therapist said I should try to be more open about my feelings.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's good advice.

dialogue.speaker: Shauna
dialogue.line: Yeah, but then she said I should play hard to get with my emotions. Now I'm ignoring my sadness to make it more interested in me.

jokes.text: Okay, he didn't watch out for his brother. You know, I'm not having this conversation with you again. That family is garbage.
jokes.setup: Ann defends Riggins taking the fall for his brother.
jokes.punchline: 'That family is garbage' as the final word on the Riggins family is hilariously disproportionate.
jokes.explanation: 'That family is garbage' applied to fictional FNL characters with complete conviction is perfect Leslie. The escalation from a nuanced debate to a sweeping condemnation is classic. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you are a beautiful, talented, brilliant, powerful musk ox. You are a goddess. A warrior. You are also a friend.

jokes.text: I think Oliver has more pressing business.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann are talking on the phone while Ann has just had a baby.
jokes.punchline: Ann's understated redirect — the baby needs to nurse — while Leslie is mid-conversation is gently funny.
jokes.explanation: Mild but functional moment. The absurdity of Leslie chatting away while Ann is postpartum is the source of the joke, and Ann's gentle redirect is charming rather than laugh-out-loud funny.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'll go back to the dentist.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But first, I'm gonna eat this entire bag of jawbreakers.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Because if I soften them up with my saliva, they're basically just regular candy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Flawless logic.

jokes.text: I almost bought a toe ring the other day. / What? Ann, you're somebody's mother. / I know. / Okay.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann are wrapping up their conversation
jokes.punchline: Leslie's horrified reaction to the toe ring — 'Ann, you're somebody's mother' — as if motherhood and toe rings are fundamentally incompatible, delivered with genuine concern
jokes.explanation: Great beat. 'Ann, you're somebody's mother' as a response to toe ring consideration is a perfect Leslie moment — her specific moral framework applied to fashion. The rhythm ('I know. / Okay.') is well-structured comic deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, there's a store called 'Tent City'? That sounds amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's right over on—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm going there right now. This is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Actually, Tom, it's not that kind of tent city. It's like a homeless encampment.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Okay, but we should talk soon, 'cause I almost bought a toe ring the other day. — What? Ann, you're somebody's mother. — I know. — Okay.
jokes.setup: Leslie is wrapping up the call with newborn Ann.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's escalating horror at the idea of Ann buying a toe ring — 'Ann, you're somebody's mother' — treats a minor fashion choice as a moral failing.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy. Leslie's disproportionate reaction to the toe ring is very funny, and Ann's simple 'I know' and Leslie's 'Okay' are perfectly understated. The brevity of the exchange is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, so Larry's research really helped us out here. I mean, I basically implemented it perfectly. My management style is really coming together.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, you didn't even read the research.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, I didn't need to. I have instincts. Natural instincts. This is what happens when you let Tom Haverford do what he does best.

jokes.text: When it's all said and done, there were a few mazes I'd cheated on. Also, the inside of my mouth is black and hot.
jokes.setup: Andy is grateful to Ron for taking him back to the dentist.
jokes.punchline: Andy's confession that he cheated on some magazine mazes — following Ron's earlier observation that they were different pictures entirely — plus 'the inside of my mouth is black and hot' is a great closing non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback with dark implications — Andy cheated on mazes that Ron told him were completely different pictures, meaning he was cheating on something that wasn't even a real puzzle. The confession is wonderfully bizarre. 'The inside of my mouth is black and hot' as a coda is a perfect Andy non-sequitur that adds unexpected physical comedy information. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann is just... she's the best. She's like if a human could be a well-organized binder. She's smart, she's kind, she's got this perfect blonde hair that just falls exactly where it should. And she's got this way of making you feel like you're the only person in the room, even when you're being completely ridiculous. Which I often am.

jokes.text: So do I strip down to my underwear, or all the way naked?
jokes.setup: Andy is presumably in the dentist's office.
jokes.punchline: Andy's complete confusion about dental procedure protocol — imagining it requires stripping — is perfect Andy logic.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant in its economy. The question implies Andy has completely misunderstood what going to the dentist involves, and the escalation (underwear vs. fully naked) suggests he's genuinely thought about which is more appropriate. Maximum funny per word. Pure Andy Dwyer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tim Riggins is overrated. Yes, he's attractive, but he's a classic example of the troubled bad boy archetype that enables toxic masculinity in sports culture.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, he has a heart of gold.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A heart of gold? Ann, the man lived in a trailer and kept making the same mistakes over and over. That's not romantic, that's a cautionary tale. I have binders full of evidence documenting his poor decision-making skills and how they negatively impacted the entire Dillon community.

jokes.text: I'm getting some for a 30-year-old who works for me, so I can bring some home for you too.
jokes.setup: Ron is on the phone with Diane, buying ice cream.
jokes.punchline: Ron matter-of-factly describing Andy as 'a 30-year-old who works for me' to explain why he's buying ice cream — treating it as a normal professional interaction.
jokes.explanation: Ron's deadpan categorization of Andy — needing ice cream, is a 30-year-old, works for Ron — delivered as if these are unremarkable facts to mention to his wife. The joke is in the normalizing of the absurd. Strong economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann is thinking about getting a toe ring.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A TOE RING, Ben!

jokes.text: Gentlemen, I've won two online satellite Jamaican poker tournaments. I can tell that you're bluffing. — Your Pawnee business license has lapsed, which negates most of the deals you've made this year. — I'm guessing you're pretty bad at poker. — I am. And I was bluffing about winning those tournaments.
jokes.setup: Harvey claims he can read bluffs from his poker experience; Larry actually does have leverage.
jokes.punchline: Harvey was right — they were bluffing (though wrong that it wouldn't work), and then admits he was lying about the poker tournaments. The double-deception is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured deception cascade. Harvey correctly identifies the bluff but still loses; then admits the poker credentials were themselves a bluff. 'I am. And I was bluffing about winning those tournaments.' as a two-part confession is excellent. The self-undermining structure is satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I cheated on my wife with the hygienist. And let me tell you something about my mouth—it's like a crime scene in there. My gums look like a murdered steak.

jokes.text: First off, I need to know where you got these zebra-print pillows. Second of all, I got a Tin Cup Blu-Ray itching for a Rene Russo signature. — Tom.
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to negotiate a fair deal with Harvey.
jokes.punchline: Tom has immediately pivoted to interior design questions and attempting to get Rene Russo memorabilia signed — recalling Harvey's earlier mention of renting tents to her.
jokes.explanation: Great callback. Tom has been filing away Harvey's Rene Russo claim since early in the episode and is now leveraging it for a signature. The specificity of 'Tin Cup Blu-Ray' as the vehicle for the autograph is a perfect Tom detail. Ben's one-word 'Tom.' as the punchline/correction is efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me I have to floss every day?

dialogue.speaker: Dentist
dialogue.line: Yes, it's important for your oral health.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But I only eat once a day... sometimes twice if there's a waffle nearby.

dialogue.speaker: Dentist
dialogue.line: That's not how flossing works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So it's not like... a schedule thing? Like, I don't have to wait 24 hours between flossing sessions?

jokes.text: And Larry, he's the guy that brought you down, and he's gonna be watching you like a hawk. — Oh, hey. I'm Larry. Great to know you. I love tent world. — God! Can you just be cool for one second?
jokes.setup: Ben sets Larry up as the threatening enforcer who will monitor Harvey.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately undermines the intimidating moment by being completely un-menacing — 'I'm Larry. Great to know you. I love tent world.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke. The setup is Ben building Larry up as an enforcer, the punchline is Larry's instant deflation of that image with his complete inability to be intimidating. 'I love tent world' is the perfect anti-tough-guy statement. 'God! Can you just be cool for one second?' is a great reaction. High structure and character integration scores. One of the episode's best Larry moments.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So when I go to the dentist, do I need to take all my clothes off?

dialogue.speaker: Dentist/Other Character
dialogue.line: No, just your shirt.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, okay. And my pants?

dialogue.speaker: Dentist/Other Character
dialogue.line: No, you can keep your pants on.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So just the shirt? What about underwear?

jokes.text: Okay, black coffee with extra grounds. Gross. For April. And a mocha ice blended for Donna.
jokes.setup: Leslie returns to the office with apology drinks.
jokes.punchline: April's order — black coffee with extra grounds, which Leslie immediately editorializes as 'Gross' — is a perfect April detail.
jokes.explanation: Quick character joke — April's order perfectly encapsulates her personality (dark, intense, unpleasant to everyone else). Leslie's interjection 'Gross' is honest and funny.

jokes.text: We love your crazy ass too, Knope. / I think you're fine. Like a solid B-minus. / Great. I'll take it.
jokes.setup: Leslie apologizes and says she loves Donna and April
jokes.punchline: April's expression of affection is 'I think you're fine. Like a solid B-minus.' — her highest praise is a mediocre grade, delivered flatly
jokes.explanation: Excellent April moment. 'A solid B-minus' as her maximum expression of friendship warmth is perfectly in character — and Leslie's cheerful 'Great. I'll take it.' shows she understands and accepts the April-language translation. Great character economy.

dialogue.speaker: Harvey
dialogue.line: I've been playing poker since I was a kid. I'm really good at it.

dialogue.speaker: Other Character
dialogue.line: Really? What's your biggest win?

dialogue.speaker: Harvey
dialogue.line: Okay, I lied. I've never played poker in my life.

jokes.text: [April and Donna present Leslie with a stuffed bunny with Ann's voice] Press the paw. Hi, Leslie. It's Ann. I love you, and everything's gonna be okay.
jokes.setup: April and Donna comfort Leslie over missing Ann.
jokes.punchline: Their solution — a stuffed bunny with a recorded Ann message — is unexpectedly sweet and funny because it comes from April and Donna, who both pretend not to care.
jokes.explanation: The emotional and comedic payoff of the Galentine's Day B-plot. The joke is that April and Donna — who both just walked out on Leslie — put in this effort anyway. The visual of the bunny is sweet and the recorded Ann message is touching. High earned-vs-cheap score because the warmth of the gesture is fully justified by the episode's setup.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, Larry's being nice to people? What is happening right now? Is this a prank? Did someone put him up to this?

jokes.text: Mm, you touch me and I stab the bunny.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to initiate a five-minute hug (her tradition with Ann).
jokes.punchline: April's immediate threat to harm the Ann bunny if Leslie tries to hug her is the perfect April rejection of sentimentality.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The threat to 'stab the bunny' as the consequence of a hug attempt is perfectly April — it's darkly funny, specific (stabbing vs. other violence), and the hostage-taking of the emotional gift is a brilliant move. Maximum economy: nine words that tell you everything about April. Immediately iconic and highly quotable. This approaches the 8.0 anchor's level of craft.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're like a five-year-old who just learned a bunch of big words and won't shut up about them.

jokes.text: I'm just an impartial bunny, but I think Ann sucks. Also -- I'm the zodiac killer.
jokes.setup: April is 'voicing' the Ann bunny after Leslie leaves.
jokes.punchline: April uses the bunny to deliver anti-Ann commentary, then escalates to the bunny claiming to be the Zodiac Killer.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. April ventriloquizing the Ann bunny to express her actual feelings ('I think Ann sucks') is brilliant, but the Zodiac Killer escalation is a masterpiece of absurdist dark comedy. 'I'm just an impartial bunny' as the setup is perfect — establishing a pretense of objectivity before revealing pure April. The Zodiac Killer claim is completely random and completely April. One of the episode's top moments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm so sorry for everything I've put you all through.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Oh honey, we know you didn't mean it. You're forgiven.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'd say you're like a 6 out of 10 friend.

jokes.text: And Larry, by the way, you're looking in the wrong spot. Your inhaler is hidden under the pile of pistachio shells on my desk, obviously. — Okay, well, that's funny, 'cause I'm terribly allergic to pistachios.
jokes.setup: Larry is having an asthma attack looking for his inhaler.
jokes.punchline: Tom casually reveals he hid Larry's inhaler under pistachio shells — to which Larry reveals he's allergic to pistachios. Tom's hiding spot is actually actively harming Larry.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed dark comedy escalation. The reveal that Tom hid the inhaler under something Larry is allergic to — while Larry is having a breathing episode — is both funny and alarming. 'Okay, well, that's funny, 'cause...' is the perfect understated setup. 'Obviously' is a great Tom add.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what is this?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We got you a Build-A-Bear Workshop bear.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: We recorded a message inside it.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's so sweet!

dialogue.speaker: Build-A-Bear
dialogue.line: Hi Ann, it's me, Ann. I'm your new friend and I love you.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We thought you'd like to have someone around who's as annoying as you are.

jokes.text: Classic.
jokes.setup: Larry reveals he's allergic to the pistachios covering his inhaler.
jokes.punchline: Tom's single-word response — 'Classic' — treating a medical emergency as a satisfying narrative beat.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word. Tom's 'Classic' as a response to a crisis he caused is perfectly callous and perfectly Tom. The word does enormous work: it treats the situation as a recurring bit, implies Tom has done similar things before, and shows zero concern. The economy score is essentially perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How about a five-minute hug?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If you do that, I will destroy whatever gift you give me.

jokes.text: I like Larry. He is a good friend and a fine man with an inexplicably gorgeous wife — I mean, to the point where it makes no sense at all. Sorry. Getting off track. He is a nice person, and we should all stand up and say, 'I...'
jokes.setup: Ben makes a speech defending Larry.
jokes.punchline: Ben's sincere speech is derailed by his genuine bafflement at Gayle's attractiveness — 'to the point where it makes no sense at all' is an escalation beyond the standard 'inexplicably gorgeous wife' joke.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Ben's earlier 'I don't care who knows... as long as no one knows' joke. The speech is sweet but derailed by the Gayle observation, which escalates from 'inexplicably gorgeous' to 'to the point where it makes no sense at all' — the second clause is the joke. The 'Sorry. Getting off track.' shows Ben's self-awareness without changing course. Strong callback and good escalation.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This bear is Ann. Look at its stupid face. And its stupid body. And its stupid everything. It's just sitting there being Ann.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to torture it. I'm going to pull off all its limbs and hide the body in the woods where no one will ever find it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've done it before.

jokes.text: I like Larry. He is a good friend and a fine man with an inexplicably gorgeous wife — I mean, to the point where it makes no sense at all. Sorry. Getting off track. He is a nice person, and we should all stand up and say, 'I...'
jokes.setup: Ben's big moment — standing up for Larry
jokes.punchline: Ben undermines his own passionate defense of Larry by getting completely derailed by the Gayle mystery ('inexplicably gorgeous wife — to the point where it makes no sense at all'), then trying to restart the speech
jokes.explanation: Great payoff for Ben's earlier talking head. His public declaration of Larry-appreciation is both brave and immediately compromised by his inability to not mention the Gayle mystery. 'To the point where it makes no sense at all' as a repeated refrain about someone's wife is darkly funny. The speech structure — disrupted by a derailment, then attempted restart — is well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Your inhaler is under those pistachio shells.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What? No! I'm allergic to pistachios!

jokes.text: Ben! No! What are you doing? — Uh, he's embarrassing himself and throwing away his career. — Sweetheart, stop. — O, captain, my captain. — What is happening? — Larry is my friend.
jokes.setup: Ben stands on a desk to make his Larry speech (implied by 'O Captain My Captain').
jokes.punchline: Ben's Dead Poets Society moment about Larry — standing on a desk yelling 'O, captain, my captain' — is simultaneously earnest and utterly ridiculous, with everyone around him horrified.
jokes.explanation: The physical escalation — Ben standing on a desk to deliver a speech about Larry — is a great visual payoff. Tom's 'he's embarrassing himself and throwing away his career' is exactly right as a straight reaction. Leslie's 'Sweetheart, stop' captures her horror at the professionalism breach while still being affectionate. 'O, captain, my captain' is perfectly absurd in context.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't understand how Larry is married. Like, I genuinely don't. Every time I see him, he's either covered in food or he's said something that would make a normal person want to leave him. And yet, there he is, married to a woman who apparently loves him. It defies logic.

jokes.text: Got so startled I tooted.
jokes.setup: Larry is moved by Ben's speech and apparently startled.
jokes.punchline: Larry's involuntary flatulence in an emotional moment — delivered with his characteristic sweet obliviousness — is the perfect Larry Garry button to the episode.
jokes.explanation: The ultimate Larry fart callback — Tom predicted it at the start, they faked one in the middle, and now the real one happens at the episode's emotional climax. The word 'tooted' is perfectly Larry — infantile and unself-conscious. The comedy is in the timing: the sincerest moment of the episode is punctured by Larry's body. High character integration and strong structural callback payoff. 'Come on, man' / 'Oh...' / 'Gross!' triple reaction from the others is the ideal button.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: O Captain! My Captain! That's what Larry is to us. He's the captain of our ship, and we should seize the day and carpe diem the heck out of this situation. We need to stand on our desks and show our respect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, that's beautiful, but also completely insane.

tmdb_overview: Leslie helps organize the high school's Senior Prom, and battles with Ron over the future employment of a bright high school senior. Andy takes an unwilling April as his date, and Tom is tasked with DJ'ing and agrees to let Ben help.
insight: Holiday-themed escalation carries 84 jokes across 22 minutes despite middling 72.8 score.
